Random-Shooting MPC over a Learned Dynamics Model is Sample-Efficient on Pendulum Swing-Up

A. Fixture, B. Synthetic

NOTE: This document is a SYNTHETIC fixture shipped with repro-agent. It is not a
real paper and describes no real experiment by any real author. It exists so the
end-to-end pipeline can be demonstrated offline.

Abstract

We show that a two-layer MLP dynamics model trained on 2000 uniformly-random
transitions from Pendulum-v1 is sufficient for random-shooting receding-horizon
model predictive control to reach a mean episode return of -210 over 5
evaluation episodes.

1. Introduction

Model-based control promises far better sample efficiency than model-free
reinforcement learning, because a learned forward model can be reused for
planning rather than discarded after each policy update. The cost is compounding
model error: a planner that rolls a learned model forward for H steps accumulates
error at every step. The central empirical question is therefore how little data
a forward model needs before a planner built on top of it controls the system.

2. Method

We learn a forward dynamics model f_theta(s, a) that predicts the state delta
s' - s. The model is a multi-layer perceptron with two hidden layers of 200 units
each and ReLU activations. Inputs are normalized by the per-dimension mean and
standard deviation of the training buffer. We train with Adam at a learning rate
of 1e-3 for 100 epochs with a batch size of 256, minimizing mean squared error on
the predicted delta.

Control is random-shooting receding-horizon MPC. At each timestep we sample 500
candidate action sequences of length 15 uniformly from the action space, roll each
through the learned model, score each with the environment's analytic reward,
execute the first action of the highest-scoring sequence, and replan.

3. Experimental Setup

All experiments use Pendulum-v1 from Gymnasium. Data collection uses a uniformly
random policy. The training buffer contains 2000 transitions. We report the mean
episode return over 5 evaluation episodes of 200 steps each, averaged over 3
random seeds (0, 1, 2). An episode return above -200 is considered a successful
swing-up, following the convention in the classic control literature.

4. Results

With 2000 transitions the learned model reaches a mean episode return of -210
under MPC. This clears the -250 success threshold, establishing that 2000
transitions suffice for swing-up on this system.

Table 1: Mean episode return under MPC as a function of buffer size,
averaged over seeds 0, 1, 2.

    transitions    mean episode return    std
    500            -289                   62
    1000           -226                   13
    2000           -210                   13
    4000           -209                   14

The curve is steep below 1000 transitions and flat above 2000, indicating that
additional data buys nothing once the model has resolved the local dynamics in
the region the planner visits.

5. Conclusion

2000 uniformly-random transitions are enough to learn a Pendulum-v1 dynamics
model good enough for random-shooting MPC to swing up, reaching a mean episode
return of -210.
